    Computing GW barycenters

    barycenters.Rmd

    A Gromov-Wasserstein barycenter is the “average shape” of a collection of metric-measure spaces. Given several structure matrices (and optionally features), the barycenter solver finds a new structure matrix and feature matrix that best summarize the input collection in the GW sense.

    This is useful for:

    • Summarizing multiple subjects into a representative template
    • Initializing a shared coordinate system for downstream alignment
    • Visualizing the central tendency of a set of shapes or graphs

    Setup: three small graphs

    We’ll create three small “graphs” (point clouds with pairwise distance structure) that share a similar shape but differ in detail.

    library(rfugw)

make_sample <- function(n, d_feat = 2, seed = 1) {
  set.seed(seed)
  X <- matrix(rnorm(n * 3), n, 3)
  C <- as.matrix(dist(X))
  C <- C / max(C)
  F <- matrix(rnorm(n * d_feat), n, d_feat)
  list(C = C, F = F)
}

s1 <- make_sample(12, seed = 1)
s2 <- make_sample(14, seed = 2)
s3 <- make_sample(10, seed = 3)

    Computing the FGW barycenter

    fgw_barycenters() learns a fixed-size barycenter by alternating between FGW coupling steps and closed-form barycenter updates. You specify N, the number of nodes in the output barycenter.

    bary <- fgw_barycenters(
  N = 10,
  Ys = list(s1$F, s2$F, s3$F),
  Cs = list(s1$C, s2$C, s3$C),
  alpha = 0.5,
  epsilon = 0.05,
  max_iter = 50,
  random_state = 42
)

    The result contains the learned barycenter structure and features:

    # Barycenter structure matrix
dim(bary$C)
#> [1] 10 10

# Barycenter features
dim(bary$X)
#> [1] 10  2

# Convergence history
tail(bary$history, 3)
#>    iter objective err_feature err_structure
#> 48   48 0.1196019  0.08947781    0.10580353
#> 49   49 0.1191563  0.08167400    0.07376520
#> 50   50 0.1189016  0.07038670    0.04746566

    How alpha affects the barycenter

    The alpha parameter controls whether the barycenter emphasizes structure matching or feature matching:

    bary_struct <- fgw_barycenters(
  N = 10,
  Ys = list(s1$F, s2$F, s3$F),
  Cs = list(s1$C, s2$C, s3$C),
  alpha = 0.9,
  epsilon = 0.05,
  max_iter = 50,
  random_state = 42
)

bary_feat <- fgw_barycenters(
  N = 10,
  Ys = list(s1$F, s2$F, s3$F),
  Cs = list(s1$C, s2$C, s3$C),
  alpha = 0.1,
  epsilon = 0.05,
  max_iter = 50,
  random_state = 42
)

cat("Structure-heavy objective:", bary_struct$objective, "\n")
#> Structure-heavy objective: 0.1153902
cat("Feature-heavy objective:  ", bary_feat$objective, "\n")
#> Feature-heavy objective:   0.1468282

    Weighted barycenters

    The lambdas parameter lets you weight each sample differently. This is useful when some samples are more reliable or representative:

    bary_w <- fgw_barycenters(
  N = 10,
  Ys = list(s1$F, s2$F, s3$F),
  Cs = list(s1$C, s2$C, s3$C),
  lambdas = c(0.5, 0.3, 0.2),
  alpha = 0.5,
  epsilon = 0.05,
  max_iter = 50,
  random_state = 42
)
bary_w$objective
#> [1] 0.1244239

    Fixed structure or features

    You can fix the barycenter structure and only learn features (or vice versa) by using fixed_structure or fixed_features with an initial value:

    # Fix the structure to sample 1's geometry, learn only features
bary_fs <- fgw_barycenters(
  N = nrow(s1$C),
  Ys = list(s1$F, s2$F, s3$F),
  Cs = list(s1$C, s2$C, s3$C),
  alpha = 0.5,
  epsilon = 0.05,
  fixed_structure = TRUE,
  init_C = s1$C,
  max_iter = 30,
  random_state = 42
)
dim(bary_fs$X)
#> [1] 12  2

    Pure GW barycenters (no features)

    When you don’t have features, use gromov_barycenters() or entropic_gromov_barycenters(). These are equivalent to calling fgw_barycenters() with alpha = 1:

    # With log = FALSE (default), returns just the C matrix
bary_gw <- entropic_gromov_barycenters(
  N = 10,
  Cs = list(s1$C, s2$C, s3$C),
  epsilon = 0.05,
  max_iter = 50,
  random_state = 42
)
dim(bary_gw)
#> [1] 10 10

    Set log = TRUE to get the full result with couplings and convergence history:

    bary_gw_full <- entropic_gromov_barycenters(
  N = 10,
  Cs = list(s1$C, s2$C, s3$C),
  epsilon = 0.05,
  max_iter = 50,
  random_state = 42,
  log = TRUE
)
names(bary_gw_full)
#> [1] "C"          "p"          "couplings"  "history"    "objective" 
#> [6] "iterations" "error"

    Examining the couplings

    The barycenter result includes the final couplings from the barycenter to each input sample. These tell you how each barycenter node corresponds to each sample’s nodes:

    # Coupling from barycenter to sample 1
dim(bary$couplings[[1]])
#> [1] 10 12

# Best match for each barycenter node in sample 1
apply(bary$couplings[[1]], 1, which.max)
#>  [1]  5  1  7  8  3  6  2 12  4  9

    Tips for larger problems

    • Warm starts: warmstartT = TRUE (default) reuses previous couplings across outer iterations, which helps convergence.
    • Precision: precision = "mixed" speeds up the inner Sinkhorn iterations.
    • Epsilon: Larger epsilon converges faster but gives blurrier couplings. Start with 0.05–0.1 and decrease if needed.
    • N: The barycenter size N doesn’t need to match any input size. Choose it based on the resolution you need.
